title: La Cegua: The Shrouded Specter
summary: A young man encounters a beautiful woman on a dark road, only to discover she is La Cegua — a veiled spirit whose terrifying face beneath her shawl punishes the unfaithful and the arrogant.
full_text:
There was a time when the roads outside Masaya were treacherous after dark, not for the bandits or wild dogs, but for something far worse. The old women of the barrio would warn: 'Never approach a lone woman on the road at night. Never trust beauty that appears where no beauty should be.'

Carlos was a vain young man, beloved by the girls of his village and proud of it. One evening, returning late from a dance in Granada, he was riding his horse along the moonlit road when he spotted a figure walking ahead — a woman in a white dress, her face hidden beneath a dark rebozo shawl. She moved with a grace that made his heart quicken.

'Where are you headed, senorita?' he called out, reining his horse beside her. 'Let me give you a ride. A beautiful woman should not walk alone.'

The figure stopped and turned toward him. Even through the shawl, he could feel her gaze. 'You think me beautiful?' she asked, her voice soft as silk. 'Then you must see my face.'

She reached up and slowly drew back the rebozo. Carlos screamed. Beneath the veil was no woman's face but the skull of a horse, hollow-eyed and grinning, its teeth blackened and enormous. The stench of death washed over him. His horse bolted in terror, throwing Carlos into the dust.

When the villagers found him at dawn, he was huddled against a tree, trembling, his hair turned white. He never again looked at a woman without first seeing the shadow of that veil.

The elders said La Cegua appears to men who are unfaithful to their wives or who disrespect women. She is the spirit of a young bride who died of grief when her husband abandoned her on their wedding night. Now she wanders the roads, offering her beauty as a test. Those who pass with humility see only a woman in mourning. Those who approach with lust or arrogance see what lies beneath — and never forget it.

To this day, horsemen in the countryside still tie red ribbons to their reins and whisper a prayer before traveling after dark. For La Cegua walks the roads of Nicaragua, and she is patient, and she remembers every slight.
moral: Disrespect and infidelity will be met with consequences more lasting than any wound of the flesh.

title: La Trola: The Deceiver
summary: La Trola is a cunning shapeshifting spirit who lures travelers into the wilderness with false promises, teaching a timeless lesson about the dangers of greed and trusting strangers.
full_text:
In the hills outside Esteli, where the coffee plantations give way to wild forest, there are paths that no map records. The farmers know them, though they will not speak of them openly. They say these paths appear only to those who are looking for something they should not want.

Old Teresa kept the village well supplied with herbs and remedies. One afternoon a stranger came to her door — a well-dressed man with a silver-tongued smile and a bundle of coins. 'I am looking for a guide,' he said. 'I have heard there are rare orchids deep in the mountains. I will pay handsomely for someone who knows the trails.'

Teresa studied the man. His clothes were too fine for the dust of Esteli. His shoes were unmarked by any road. And his shadow, she noticed, did not quite match his shape. 'I am too old for such journeys,' she told him. 'But my grandson Miguel knows the mountains well.'

The stranger smiled wider. 'Then send the boy. I will make it worth his trouble — worth all your troubles.'

That night Teresa told Miguel: 'If the stranger comes, go with him, but do not follow him past the second river. And whatever he offers you, do not accept anything that is not food or water. La Trola does not pay her debts.'

Miguel, being young, thought his grandmother superstitious. When the stranger came at dawn, Miguel followed him eagerly. The man knew the trails surprisingly well for a foreigner, and he spoke of gold hidden in caves, of treasures left by the old kingdoms. At the second river, Miguel stopped.

'Wait,' he said. 'This is far enough.'

The stranger turned, and for a moment his face flickered — like heat over sun-baked stone. His smile was too wide. His eyes were not right. 'Come,' said La Trola, dropping the pretense of a human voice. 'We are so close to everything you have ever wanted.'

Miguel crossed himself and turned back. He heard La Trola shriek behind him — a sound like tearing metal — but she did not follow across the running water. When he reached the village, the stranger's coins in his pocket had turned to dead leaves.

Teresa simply nodded. 'La Trola is older than the mountains,' she said. 'She knows what every person desires, and she uses it. The only defense is knowing your own heart well enough to see when it is being used against you.'

And so the people of Esteli still tell the tale: the paths that promise shortcuts to fortune are the ones most likely to lead you where you will never return.
moral: Greed blinds us to the traps laid in our path, and the sweetest promises often conceal the deepest dangers.

title: El Boyo: The Mournful Ghost
summary: El Boyo is a sorrowful ghost haunting the rivers and swamps of Nicaragua, the restless spirit of a drowned man whose eerie wailing warns travelers away from dangerous waters.
full_text:
The Río Tuma winds through the lowlands like a sleeping serpent, its waters dark and slow beneath walls of ceiba and ceibilla. In the villages along its banks, children are taught early: do not fish alone after sunset. Do not answer a voice that calls from the river in the hours before dawn. That voice is El Boyo.

No one remembers his true name. Some say he was a fisherman who drowned in a sudden flood, his body never recovered by his family. Others say he was a young man who crossed the wrong curandero and was cursed to wander the waters forever. Whatever the truth, his grief is real. On still nights, when the mist hangs low over the river, you can hear him — a long, rising wail that begins as a human cry and ends in something not quite human at all.

Sofia and her brother Juan were returning late from a festival in Wiwilí when their mule refused to cross the old wooden bridge over the Tuma. The animal brayed and stamped, its eyes rolling white with terror. Then they heard it — a sound rising from the water, a moan that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere.

'Mama says if you hear El Boyo, you must not look at the water,' Sofia whispered, gripping her brother's arm. 'You must walk forward and not stop.'

But Juan, who did not believe in such things, stepped to the bridge railing and peered into the darkness below. There, in the swirling current, he saw a shape — pale, translucent, rising from the river like smoke. It had the form of a man, but its face was a void, a hollow nothingness that seemed to pull at his very soul.

Juan could not move. He could not scream. He felt his feet lifting from the planks, felt the cold river water climbing toward him, though the river was ten feet below. Only when Sofia grabbed his arm with both hands and dragged him backward did the spell break. The shape sank beneath the water with a sound like a sigh.

They ran. They did not stop until they reached the village, where the old men shook their heads knowingly. 'El Boyo was showing you what drowning feels like,' one said. 'He is lonely. He wants company. But his companionship is death.'

Now, when travelers cross the bridge over the Tuma, they leave small offerings — a candle, a handful of tobacco, a coin tossed into the current. Not to honor El Boyo, but to remind him that the living remember him. For even ghosts, they say, are comforted by the knowledge that someone, somewhere, still cares that they existed.
moral: The dead who are not properly mourned become dangers to the living; remembrance is a form of mercy.

title: Viejito del Monte: The Little Old Man of the Mountain
summary: The Viejito del Monte is a small, ancient nature-spirit of the Nicaraguan highlands who rewards those who respect the forest and punishes those who despoil it.
full_text:
In the cloud forests of the Diriamba highlands, where the trees wear veils of moss and the air tastes of wet earth, the old ones say there lives a spirit no taller than a child's knee. They call him El Viejito del Monte — the Little Old Man of the Mountain — and though his appearance is small, his power reaches from root to crown of every tree in the forest.

He is ancient beyond reckoning, older than the Spanish, older than the Chorotega, older perhaps than the mountains themselves. His beard is white as orchid root. His clothes are woven from bark and lichen. His eyes are the deep green of forest shadow, and they see everything that happens beneath the canopy.

Diego was a woodcutter from Nandaime who had been hired to clear a section of hillside for a new cattle ranch. He had been warned by the old women: 'Take only what you need. Leave the big ceibas. The Viejito del Monte lives in the largest one at the top of the ridge.'

Diego laughed. He was a practical man, and practical men do not take orders from spirits they have never seen. With his axe over his shoulder, he climbed the ridge at dawn. The forest was thick and silent, but Diego did not notice the silence. He did not notice the way the birds stopped singing as he passed, or the way the trail seemed to curve back on itself when he was not watching.

He reached the great ceiba at the ridge's peak and raised his axe. But before the blade fell, he heard a voice — thin and dry, like leaves scraping stone. 'Are you certain about that, my son?'

Diego spun around. Sitting on a root, no larger than a loaf of bread, was a tiny old man with a white beard and eyes like deep wells. He was calmly smoking a pipe made from a hollow reed, and he regarded Diego with an expression of patient curiosity.

'Who are you?' Diego demanded.

'I am the one who lives here,' the Viejito said. 'As the trees live here, and the birds, and the rain. This forest is not yours to take. But if you must cut, cut only what is fallen. Leave the standing trees. They are my bones.'

Diego, shaken but still defiant, swung his axe at the root where the old man sat. The axe passed through him like smoke, and Diego stumbled. When he looked up, the Viejito del Monte was gone. And in his place, every tree on the ridge had turned its trunk to face Diego, and every branch had lowered like an arm pointing toward the path back down.

Diego ran. He did not stop running until he reached the village, where he threw his axe into the river and swore he would never cut a living tree again. And from that day, he became the forest's most devoted protector — planting seedlings where others cleared, speaking to the trees as neighbors.

The Viejito del Monte was seen again, the old women said, sitting on the same root, smoking his pipe, with a look of quiet satisfaction. He does not ask much — only that we remember the forest is alive, and that we treat it as we would treat any elder: with respect, with restraint, and with gratitude.
moral: The forest remembers every axe; treat its ancient beings with reverence, and they will shelter you in return.
